justifications.functional_suitability: All functional requirements are comprehensively supported: Fraud Scoring Engine (with Rule Engine and Inference Client) handles real-time scoring (R-01), Case Management App manages analyst reviews (R-02), and Model Hot-Loader Component in ONNX Model Sidecar enables zero-downtime model updates from Amazon S3 (R-03).
justifications.performance_efficiency: P99 < 50ms at 3,000 TPS is well-supported: Go-based Fraud Scoring Engine communicates via UDS/localhost gRPC with the C++ ONNX Model Sidecar, FeatureStore Table uses DynamoDB provisioned reads, and Audit Logger offloads audit persistence asynchronously via DynamoDB Streams and EventBridge.
justifications.compatibility: Application Load Balancer terminates gRPC over mTLS 1.3 from Payment Gateway, while Tokenization Gateway Client interfaces with Card Schemes / Tokenization Service over mTLS. Event Schema Registry validates decision payloads using JSON Schema.
justifications.usability: UI SPA Component (React) explicitly provides fraud analysts with a dashboard displaying masked card details and workflow updates. However, dedicated monitoring and operational workflows specifically tailored for ML Engineers lack explicit interface mechanisms.
justifications.reliability: High reliability is provided by Cross-Region Replication, pgBouncer, Dead Letter Queue Handler, and circuit breakers in Feature Assembler. However, the concrete fail-open or timeout bypass mechanism to unblock payments within 1 minute (R-07) during complete scoring engine outages is not explicitly detailed.
justifications.security: Meets PCI-DSS Level 1: AWS WAFv2 inspects ingress, API Controller enforces OIDC/MFA and RBAC, Tokenization Gateway Client masks PAN data, and Amazon S3 Bucket in Compliance Mode with AWS KMS guarantees immutable, tamper-evident 7-year audit retention.
justifications.maintainability: Operable by three engineers due to managed serverless/container infrastructure (ECS Fargate, RDS Proxy, DynamoDB). Decoupling the Model Hot-Loader Component and ONNX Model Sidecar from Fraud Scoring Engine enables independent, zero-downtime updates and testing.
justifications.portability: Workloads run in standard OCI containers on ECS Fargate. The architecture targets AWS eu-west-1 as required, though deep reliance on proprietary services (DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, S3 Object Lock) limits portability to other cloud providers without refactoring.

PERF-01.justification: The Go scoring engine uses in-memory rules, concurrent DynamoDB feature assembly via VPC endpoints, and UDS/localhost gRPC to a C++ ONNX runtime avoiding GC pauses, reliably achieving sub-50ms P99 latency at 3,000 TPS.
sensitivity_points: DynamoDB point-read latency and connection pooling under 3,000 TPS peak
Inter-process communication overhead between Go engine and ONNX sidecar
tradeoffs: Localhost sidecar deployment increases container memory footprint to avoid network hop latency

PERF-02.justification: Case management is completely decoupled from real-time scoring into a separate Node.js/React container on ECS, served by Amazon RDS PostgreSQL with RDS Proxy/pgBouncer, ensuring zero interference with scoring latency.
sensitivity_points: Database connection exhaustion on RDS during surge analyst activity
tradeoffs: Separate database infrastructure guarantees scoring isolation but consumes part of the monthly budget

AVAIL-01.justification: While ECS Fargate provides auto-recovery and ALB performs health checks, the architecture lacks an explicit gateway-level fallback path or fail-open mechanism to decide and audit payments within 1 minute if scoring tasks crash.
sensitivity_points: ALB health check interval and target group failover detection timing
tradeoffs: Strict inline scoring prevents unauthorized approvals but risks transaction timeouts if engine crashes

AVAIL-02.justification: Audit logging is fully decoupled from synchronous scoring using asynchronous signing and buffering, DynamoDB Streams, and EventBridge with Dead Letter Queues, guaranteeing zero request stalling or lost audit records during downstream failures.
sensitivity_points: Asynchronous buffer limits and DLQ retention during sustained S3 outages
tradeoffs: Eventual consistency for audit logs preserves strict sub-50ms transaction latency

MOD-01.justification: The Model Hot-Loader in the ONNX sidecar dynamically downloads verified .onnx models and manifests from S3 at runtime without container restarts, enabling zero-downtime hot-swaps, sub-5-minute rollbacks, and explicit model version tracking.
sensitivity_points: Atomic model pointer switching inside ONNX Runtime during active inference calls
tradeoffs: Dynamic runtime model loading adds sidecar complexity compared to immutable container image releases

MOD-02.justification: The Rule Engine explicitly records applied rule IDs in decision payloads. While updating compiled Go rules requires an ECS rolling deployment (well within the 1-hour window without downtime), dynamic runtime rule reloading without deployment is not modeled.
sensitivity_points: ECS rolling update duration and target group deregistration delays
tradeoffs: Compiled Go rule engine maximizes execution speed at the expense of dynamic interpretation

SEC-01.justification: Card data exposure is strictly prevented using external tokenization and UI-level masking. However, while WAF, pgaudit, and CloudWatch logs exist, an automated anomaly detection mechanism to alert on compromised analyst behavior within 15 minutes is missing.
sensitivity_points: Completeness of log collection and latency of external SIEM alerting pipelines
tradeoffs: Strict tokenization ensures PCI scope reduction but relies on external service availability

SEC-02.justification: Audit payloads containing inputs, model versions, and signed explanations are stored in Amazon S3 Object Lock Compliance Mode with KMS CMK encryption and transitioned to Glacier Flexible Archive, guaranteeing 7-year tamper-evident reproducibility within hours.
sensitivity_points: KMS key rotation policies and Glacier Flexible Archive retrieval latency
tradeoffs: Glacier tiering drastically cuts 7-year storage costs while easily meeting 1-day retrieval requirements
